summary.title: What Makes Code Hard To Read: Visual Patterns of Complexity
summary.one_liner: You learn eight visually observable code patterns (function size, novelty, grouping, conditional simplicity, gotos, nesting, variable distinction, variable liveness) that make code harder to read, drawn from Halstead metrics and SonarSource's Cognitive Complexity.
keywords: what makes code hard to read
takeaways: Halstead metrics (operators and operands counts, volume, difficulty) give a rough, language-agnostic measure of how much a function makes a reader track.
Cognitive Complexity penalizes nesting, breaks in linear flow, and mixed logical operators, but ignores function length and some exception costs.
Keep variables' live ranges short, avoid shadowing, and use visually distinct, descriptive names.
Split long function chains into well-named helpers or intermediate variables, and isolate deep nesting into functions.
Consistency with familiar code shapes reduces the reader's cognitive load; the post proposes eight patterns to apply across languages.
summary.summary: The author, after finding a high-quality but tiring codebase to audit, sets out to find objective, visual patterns that make code hard to read, since no widely accepted readability metric exists. He examines Halstead complexity metrics (counting operators and operands, with JavaScript examples measured via an online tool) and SonarSource's Cognitive Complexity whitepaper, critiquing each with code examples covering shorthand constructs, switch versus if-else, logical operator chains, exceptions, goto, and nesting. He then discusses naming, variable liveness, and familiar code patterns, and distills them into eight readability factors. The post is opinionated and explicitly flags that the field is murky.
